checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: 10M drivers pinging every 4 seconds. Where do their positions live?

options.label: PostGIS on Postgres
options.verdict: Lovely SQL ergonomics and real range queries, and it is the right first answer at low scale. It falls over here for one reason: every ping is a row write, so you are asking a disk-backed B-tree to absorb millions of writes per second.

options.label: Redis geospatial
options.verdict: A sorted set keyed by region, updated in memory. Losing a few seconds of state is survivable because every driver re-pings within 4 seconds, which is exactly why the durable store is the wrong tool for this data.

defend.prompt: What did you accept by moving locations out of Postgres?

options.label: Location state is now lossy on a Redis failure
You need a sharding scheme per city or region
Drivers and rides now live in two different stores
You can no longer answer 'who is within 3km'

defend.explain: GEOSEARCH answers proximity fine. The costs are durability, a sharding decision, and split-brain between the hot location store and the system of record.

checkpoints.title: Capacity ladder
checkpoints.prompt: 10M active drivers, each pinging every 4 seconds.

rungs.note: 10M / 4s. This is the number that rules out a row-per-ping design.
Under a minute, with ~10s per driver accept window inside it.

rungs.q: Requests in one cell when a concert empties
rungs.note: Local density, not global average, is what breaks dispatch.

checkpoints.explain: 2.5M writes/sec is a throughput problem; 100k in one cell is a hot-partition problem. They need different answers — in-memory geo for the first, queueing plus radius expansion for the second.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the dispatch read path from a ride request to an offer.
checkpoints.explain: The request is persisted by Ride Service, then handed to Kafka so a demand spike queues instead of dropping. Match Service consumes, runs GEOSEARCH against Redis, and only then reaches Notification Service. Temporal owns the offer-timeout loop, and Postgres is the system of record — neither sits on this hot path.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: Match latency went from 8 seconds to 90 seconds, in one city only.
checkpoints.explain: One city means one partition. Requests are partitioned by geohash prefix, so a local surge lands entirely on a single partition and a single consumer group — the rest of the fleet sits idle while that one backs up. The fix is more partitions for the hot prefix plus autoscaled consumers, not a bigger Redis.

wrong.Redis Geo Index: 1.2ms is healthy. The geo index is keeping up; something upstream is not handing it work fast enough.
wrong.Postgres primary: +4ms cannot explain 82 seconds. It is following the queue, not causing it.
wrong.API Gateway: Requests are arriving fine — they are waiting after they arrive.
